dedupe_keys.name: st gallen deep geothermal project induced seismicity and gas kick 2013 modelling study

description: This case study examines the St. Gallen deep geothermal project in Switzerland, which in July 2013 aimed to supply district heating and generate power. A few days after an injection test and two acid stimulations that caused only minor seismicity, a gas kick forced the operators to inject drilling mud, and several earthquakes followed on a fault several hundred metres from the well, including a felt magnitude 3.5 event. Dominik Zbinden, Antonio Pio Rinaldi, Tobias Diehl and Stefan Wiemer of ETH Zurich present a conceptual model from seismic, borehole and seismological data that links the well hydraulically to the fault, and test it with a numerical model calibrated on borehole pressure. Coverage is the St. Gallen well and nearby fault during the 2013 operations. The article appeared in Solid Earth in 2020 and is accessible online as an open access PDF in the ETH Research Collection under CC-BY-4.0 at no cost. Caveats: the gas release mechanism is a tested hypothesis, not a direct observation, and injected volumes were small (about 1,200 cubic metres). Simulation uses are induced seismicity hazard assessment and risk screening for deep geothermal heat projects. Related records: none linked on the provider's pages read on the day.
name: St. Gallen deep geothermal project induced seismicity and gas kick (2013) - modelling study
outcomes: The model reproduced the gas kick and the space-time pattern of the main seismic sequence, indicating that released overpressurised gas may have destabilised the fault and enhanced seismicity.
resources_used: Seismic and borehole data from the St. Gallen well
Numerical hydromechanical model calibrated to the injection test
